title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Washington, DC: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for the capital region: federal and data-center steel, Potomac bridges, gas mains and three building codes. Online or on site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Washington, DC: Six Days of Study for Welding Inspectors Across the District, Maryland and Northern Virginia
html:
Welding inspection in the capital region rarely stops at the District line. A single inspector can start the morning on a federal building renovation near the Mall, spend the afternoon on a data hall frame in Loudoun County, and finish the week on a utility crew in Prince George's County. Contracts across all three jurisdictions keep asking for the same personal credential: AWS Certified Welding Inspector. Atlantis NDT runs a CWI preparation course lasting six days (a 6-day plan mapped to Parts A, B and C) for welders, ironworkers, pipefitters, QC technicians, NDT technicians and engineers in the Washington area who are getting ready for the AWS examination.

Atlantis teaches; AWS certifies. The American Welding Society writes the CWI examination, administers it, grades it and grants the certification, and it decides who is eligible to sit. AWS has not approved or endorsed this course, and Atlantis never sees examination content. The complete day-by-day syllabus and AWS's published exam structure are on the national AWS CWI exam prep page; everything below is about working and testing in and around Washington.

One metro, three rulebooks

The first thing a Washington-area inspector learns is that the building code changes when you cross a river or a boundary road. Inside the District, construction follows the DC Construction Codes, with the building code published in Title 12-A of the District of Columbia Municipal Regulations and administered by the Department of Buildings. Virginia applies its Uniform Statewide Building Code everywhere in the Commonwealth, and Maryland adopts the Maryland Building Performance Standards, which counties then amend. All three are built on the International Building Code, so the structural steel welding requirements look familiar, but special inspection procedures, agency forms and who signs what vary by jurisdiction.

For a CWI the practical effect is simple. Structural welds on most permitted projects are judged against AWS D1.1, and the owner's special inspector or testing agency verifies them. The paperwork route to the building official is what differs, so an inspector who works across the metro keeps a mental map of which jurisdiction a project sits in before the first weld is checked. The examination does not test local procedures, but Part C does test whether you can find a requirement in the code quickly, and that skill transfers directly to reading three sets of local rules.

Federal owners and contract specifications

Few regions have as much construction paid for by the federal government. Agency headquarters, courthouses, laboratories, military installations and museum renovations all come with contract specifications that sit on top of the building code. Federal construction contracts usually require the contractor to run a quality control program with named inspectors, and the owner's representatives check that program rather than inspecting every weld themselves. A contractor's welding inspector on that work is expected to know the code, keep daily records and stand behind every acceptance.

For structural steel buildings, AISC 360, the specification most structural drawings cite, includes a chapter that divides inspection into quality control by the fabricator and erector and quality assurance by the owner's agency, and it points to AWS standards for how welding inspection personnel are qualified. In practice that is why so many capital-region job postings ask for a CWI by name. Read the specification on your own contract to see what it requires, because federal guide specifications are edited project by project.

The Navy adds a different layer. NAVSEA, the command that sets welding and inspection requirements for Navy ships, has its headquarters at the Washington Navy Yard, but the shipyards that apply those rules sit in Hampton Roads and elsewhere. Washington-area inspectors who travel for ship work learn quickly that Navy programs qualify inspectors under their own requirements; the CWI travels with the inspector and gives the foundation, while the yard's own qualification goes with the job.

Data halls, substations and the Dulles corridor

Northern Virginia holds one of the largest concentrations of data centers in the world, clustered around Ashburn and spreading across Loudoun, Prince William and neighboring counties. Every campus is a large welding project in disguise: structural steel frames and roof dunnage, pipe racks for chilled water and condenser loops, generator fuel systems, and electrical substations with welded steel structures. Steel fabricators, mechanical contractors and testing agencies serving those campuses keep CWIs busy on in-shop and field inspection.

The mechanical side of a data hall brings piping codes into play. Chilled water and fuel lines are commonly designed to ASME B31.9 or B31.1 depending on the owner's standard, and welders on that work are qualified under ASME Section IX. A CWI candidate whose experience is mostly on data-center piping may find the ASME selection for Part C a closer fit than the structural steel code. Two primers help here: our article on procedure specifications, qualification records and welder tests, and a summary of ASME Section IX.

Transit construction follows the same corridor. Metrorail's Silver Line now runs past Dulles Airport into Loudoun County, and station structures, pedestrian bridges and traction power facilities on projects like that are welded steel work inspected to agency specifications.

Bridges over the Potomac and the Anacostia

Water divides the region, so bridges are constant work. The District replaced the Frederick Douglass Memorial Bridge over the Anacostia with a new arch structure, and rail and highway crossings of the Potomac are under study, rehabilitation or expansion at any given time. Bridge steel is fabricated and inspected under AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, plus the owning agency's special provisions. D1.5 tightens procedure control, consumable storage and preheat, and adds a fracture control plan for members whose failure would be catastrophic. An inspector working for a bridge fabricator or for the owner's consultant needs to know which members carry those extra demands.

If bridge work is your main interest, D1.5 is a serious choice for Part C; the AWS D1.5 overview lays out how the code is organized. Many bridge fabricators supplying capital-region projects are based in Maryland, Pennsylvania and Virginia, so expect travel to shops for in-process inspection.

Gas, water and tunnel work

Older neighborhoods across the District and its inner suburbs sit on gas mains that are being replaced section by section, and steel distribution and transmission lines are joined and judged to API 1104, a standard that the federal gas pipeline regulations in 49 CFR Part 192 reference for welding qualification. Pipeline contractors and the utility's own inspectors value CWIs who can read API 1104 confidently, especially its acceptance criteria for visual and radiographic indications. The API 1104 overview is a useful starting point.

Water and sewer infrastructure brings its own steel: large-diameter pipe, pumping station piping and tunnel linings and shafts built for the region's combined sewer overflow program. Some of that work follows water-industry standards rather than AWS codes, but the inspection skills the CWI examination tests, measuring welds, recognizing discontinuities and checking work against a written requirement, apply everywhere.

Who employs CWIs between Baltimore and Fredericksburg

Employer typeTypical CWI dutiesCode most often in play
Testing and special inspection agenciesOwner's verification on buildings in DC, Maryland and Virginia; daily reports to the building officialAWS D1.1
General and steel contractors on federal workContractor quality control, welder qualification records, field weld acceptanceAWS D1.1 plus contract specifications
Data-center mechanical and structural contractorsShop and field inspection of steel frames, pipe racks and fuel and water pipingAWS D1.1 and ASME Section IX with B31 piping codes
Bridge fabricators and owner's consultantsIn-process inspection, fracture-critical member checks, record reviewAWS D1.5
Gas utilities and pipeline contractorsMain replacement and transmission welding inspectionAPI 1104

Because the region's work is spread across so many owners, inspectors here often change employers or move between agencies and contractors. The CWI belongs to the person holding it, which makes it a practical credential in a market that moves this way.

AWS District 3 and the Washington D.C. Section

AWS organizes its local sections into districts, and the capital region sits in District 3. Among the officers of the AWS Washington D.C. Section is a certification chair, the obvious person to ask about how the CWI process plays out locally. The section's recent activity shows how it works: in April 2026 it joined the district's welcome for the visiting AWS president, a tour that took in student welding competitions, local industry and a school, and each September it holds a long-running joint family picnic with the Cumberland Valley Section, most recently in Cooksville, Maryland. The section also lists an AWS student chapter at Madison Welders. Details are posted on the section's page at sections.aws.org.

Section events are the easiest way to meet working inspectors, hear about the practical exam from people who recently sat it, and learn which local agencies and fabricators are hiring. They are also where AWS Foundation scholarship information circulates for students coming up through welding programs.

Experience first: what AWS expects before you apply

The CWI is built for people who have already welded, fitted or inspected for years. AWS weighs formal education against documented welding-related work, so the more relevant schooling you have, the shorter the work history it requires. A candidate whose education ended at high school needs five years; a welding engineering or welding technology bachelor's degree cuts that to one. The full table is on the national course page, and AWS has the final word on what qualifies.

Washington has a large community of veterans and military family members, and service welding, construction or maintenance time may count if it was welding-based work that someone can verify. Federal contractors' project records, union apprenticeship logs and employer letters all help. Gather them before you start studying so that an eligibility question does not stall the application weeks before your practical date. Vision is checked separately on the current AWS form, covering near acuity and color perception.

Sitting the three parts from the capital region

AWS splits the examination three ways. Fundamentals and code application are computer-based tests booked through Prometric once AWS mails a confirmation carrying your eligibility code; Prometric seats exist throughout the metro. The practical is the part that needs planning: AWS stages it at a limited set of venues tied to its seminars, on a calendar it controls, and you measure and judge specimens using instruments AWS lays out for you. Check aws.org for the closest practical venue and its dates before committing to a study timetable.

Each part has a 72% floor, and the three scores arrive on a single AWS report. Examination charges are an AWS matter and are posted on aws.org; travel, the code book and study time are yours to budget, and the CWI cost planner lays those out. The breakdown of results by part shows which part tends to cause trouble.

Six days that fit federal schedules and data-center shifts

The six days are the same for every candidate. The opening pair of days handles Part A territory: arc processes and AWS vocabulary, joints and symbols first, then steel behavior, bend and tensile tests, the origins of each discontinuity, the NDT methods a CWI requests, shop safety and the inspector's code of conduct. Day three is a dry run of the hands-on part, reading gauges and judging profiles the way the practical demands. Day four puts candidates inside the code book they picked. Day five is mock papers against the clock for all three parts, and day six spends its hours on whatever those papers exposed, then on test-day planning and the paperwork AWS wants.

For an individual candidate

You study online at your own pace. Atlantis provides a study plan following the six days, written materials, practice questions it wrote to the published body of knowledge, and timed mock papers, and an instructor answers your questions as they come up. Nothing is scheduled, which suits inspectors on rotating shifts or long commutes around the Beltway. Practice items are Atlantis's own work; none was lifted from an AWS paper.

For a contractor or agency

A testing agency, steel contractor or mechanical contractor can host the six days on its own premises for several staff together. The practical work then uses the company's gauges and welds from its own jobs, and the code practice can follow the book the team uses every day, whether D1.1 for buildings, D1.5 for bridges or the ASME codes for piping. Each employee files a personal AWS application and has to meet the experience and eyesight rules individually.

Which Part C book suits Washington work

Choose the code you read most at work. Building and federal steel inspectors usually take D1.1; the D1.1 overview and the guide to D1.1 acceptance criteria are good primers. Bridge inspectors and fabricator QC staff should consider D1.5. Utility and pipeline inspectors fit API 1104. Data-center and plant piping inspectors should look at the ASME selection. Study the edition AWS names in its reference material, which may be older than the one in print, and practice locating tables under time pressure, because the open-book part rewards navigation more than memory.

Adding NDT methods after the CWI

Visual inspection and record review are the core of CWI work, but capital-region projects regularly need more than the eye can give: sound waves sent through full-penetration joints, iron powder that gathers at surface cracks in steel, and dye that seeps from fine openings in stainless or aluminum. Those tests are carried out by technicians whom their employer certifies under ASNT SNT-TC-1A after training, logged experience and examination. Atlantis offers SNT-TC-1A-based courses for that next step: see NDT training in Washington, DC, NDT training in Virginia, ultrasonic testing in Washington, DC, magnetic particle testing in Washington, DC and VT Level 2 training. The Practical NDT welding workshop and the free NDT practice tests help you keep inspection skills sharp.

Plan for the long term as well. A CWI lasts nine years on AWS's terms. Paperwork goes in at the three-year and six-year marks, and at nine the credential must be recertified. For a wider look at what the credential does for a career, read CWI requirements and career impact.

Requesting a quote for capital-region candidates

Tell us how many people need preparation, sketch each candidate's education and welding work history, name the Part C book each intends to choose, and note whether anyone already holds an AWS confirmation letter or a practical date. For on-site delivery, add the site address (District, Maryland or Virginia), the gauges and sample welds you can provide, and the weeks that fit your project calendar. Use the Washington, DC CWI preparation enquiry, and we reply within one business day.

Neighboring markets: CWI exam prep in Baltimore, Philadelphia and New York.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Washington, DC?
faq.a: No. Houston and Hyderabad are where Atlantis keeps offices, and nowhere in the capital region. People there prepare online and message an instructor when stuck, or a contractor brings the program onto its own site. The full outline is on the national page.
AWS. It sets eligibility, administers and grades the three-part examination, and certifies those who pass. Preparation is the part Atlantis handles.

faq.q: Do DC, Maryland and Virginia accept the same welding inspector credential?
faq.a: All three base their building codes on the International Building Code, and structural welds are generally judged against AWS D1.1. Each jurisdiction's building official decides which inspector qualifications are acceptable for special inspection, and the CWI is the credential most structural welding inspectors present.

faq.q: Which code book should a data-center piping inspector choose?
faq.a: The ASME selection, which pairs Section IX with the B31 piping codes, usually fits mechanical and fuel piping work best. Structural steel inspectors on the same campuses usually choose D1.1.

faq.q: Does working at the Washington Navy Yard qualify me to inspect Navy ships?
faq.a: No. Ships answer to NAVSEA documents, and each yard decides who may inspect under its Navy program. Hold the CWI as your own portable credential next to whatever the yard grants you.

faq.q: Where do Washington candidates take the practical?
faq.a: The practical runs on AWS dates at AWS-chosen venues, so look up the closest one on aws.org early. Fundamentals and code application are taken on a computer at a Prometric site, and the District, Maryland and Virginia all have several.

faq.q: Can military welding experience count toward eligibility?
faq.a: Possibly. AWS judges each case, looking for hands-on welding duties backed by records and a person who will confirm them. Pull together discharge papers, rating or MOS training, and the names of former supervisors.

faq.q: Are the course practice questions taken from the AWS exam?
faq.a: No. Each one was composed by Atlantis from the topic list AWS makes public. The real question bank is closed to Atlantis.

faq.q: Is there a local AWS section?
faq.a: Yes. The District 3 group serving the capital is the AWS Washington D.C. Section; it names a certification chair and posts its events at sections.aws.org.

faq.q: How do I get a price for the course?
faq.a: Every request gets its own quote. Exam charges come from AWS and sit on its website; for the remaining items, open the cost planner. Ask for a quote.
